PSE II · Chapter 29

Electromagnetic Induction

A changing flux makes an EMF

← PSE II Course

29.0 — Only Change Matters

Chapter 28 found that currents make magnetic fields. The question that ran the other way waited a decade for an answer: can a magnetic field make a current?

Michael Faraday (1791–1867), a blacksmith’s son apprenticed to a bookbinder at fourteen, educated himself from the books he bound and became Humphry Davy’s laboratory assistant at the Royal Institution. He knew from Ørsted (1820) that a current deflects a compass, and he spent ten years trying to reverse the effect. On 29 August 1831 he succeeded. Pushing a bar magnet into a coil sent a brief pulse through a galvanometer; pulling it out sent a pulse the other way; and with the magnet sitting still inside the coil, nothing flowed at all.

“Nothing is too wonderful to be true, if it be consistent with the laws of nature.” — Michael Faraday, 1849

A magnetic field makes no current. A changing one does. Joseph Henry (1797–1878) in Albany found the same effect at about the same time; Faraday published first. The unit of inductance (§29.5) carries Henry’s name.

*A note on order: in this course Chapter 29 is the last chapter. Chapter 31 already stated Faraday’s law as law (3) of §31.1; this chapter supplies the experiment behind it, and it settles two results Chapter 31 used without derivation — the magnetic energy density \(u_B\) (§29.6) and the speed of light from laws (3) and (4) (§29.7).

29.1 — Magnetic Flux

Flux Through a Loop

Section 31.1 defined the magnetic flux through a surface exactly as Chapter 23 defined the electric flux, and §28.7 showed that the flux out of any closed surface is zero. Faraday’s law uses the flux through an open surface bounded by a loop of wire:

\[\Phi_B = \int \vec B \cdot d\vec A\]

The direction of \(d\vec A\) is the surface’s normal \(\hat n\), tied to a chosen direction around the loop by the right-hand rule (§31.1). For a uniform field through a flat loop of area \(A\), with \(\theta\) the angle between \(\vec B\) and \(\hat n\):

\[\boxed{\;\Phi_B = BA\cos\theta \qquad (1\ \text{Wb} = 1\ \text{T}\cdot\text{m}^2)\;}\]

  • \(\theta = 0\): \(\Phi_B = BA\), the most the loop can hold.
  • \(\theta = 90°\): \(\Phi_B = 0\). The field lines run along the surface without piercing it.
  • \(\theta = 180°\): \(\Phi_B = -BA\). The same field threads the loop the other way, relative to the chosen \(\hat n\).

A coil of \(N\) identical turns catches the flux \(\Phi_B\) in each turn. The total, \(N\Phi_B\), is the flux linkage; it is the quantity Faraday’s law and inductance (§29.5) both use.

Electric flux (Ch 23) Magnetic flux (Ch 28–29)
Definition \(\Phi_E = \int\vec E\cdot d\vec A\) \(\Phi_B = \int\vec B\cdot d\vec A\)
Out of a closed surface \(Q_\text{enc}/\varepsilon_0\) \(0\) (§28.7)
Through a loop, changing drives a circulating \(\vec B\) (§31.2) drives a circulating \(\vec E\) (§29.2)

Example: Flux Through a Tilted Loop

A circular loop of radius \(r\) sits in a uniform field \(B\), its normal at \(\theta\) to the field. Find the flux for \(r = 0.100\) m, \(B = 0.500\) T, \(\theta = 30.0°\).

Why it matters: the field and the loop’s tilt are what can be measured; the flux is the one number Faraday’s law needs. Turned through a full circle, the flux swings from its face-on value to minus that value, and that swing is the generator of §29.2.

Step 1 — symbols. \(A = \pi r^2\), so

\[\Phi_B = B\pi r^2\cos\theta\]

Step 2 — numbers.

\[\boxed{\;\Phi_B = (0.500\ \text{T})\,\pi(0.100\ \text{m})^2\cos 30.0° = 1.36\times10^{-2}\ \text{Wb} = 13.6\ \text{mWb}\;}\]

Face-on the same loop holds \(15.7\) mWb; edge-on, zero.

Example: A Loop Around a Solenoid

A long solenoid of radius \(r_s\) with \(n\) turns per meter carries current \(I\). A circular loop of radius \(r_\ell > r_s\) surrounds it on the same axis. Find the flux through the loop for \(r_s = 5.00\) cm, \(n = 1000\) turns/m, \(I = 3.00\) A, \(r_\ell = 15.0\) cm.

Why it matters: the solenoid’s winding and current are set on the bench; the flux through the outer loop is what a pickup coil reads. Flux is counted where the field is, which is why a pickup coil does not need to fit snugly.

Step 1 — where the field is. Inside the solenoid \(B = \mu_0 nI\) (§28.6); outside, \(B \approx 0\). Only the solenoid’s cross-section carries flux, so the loop’s own area does not appear:

\[\Phi_B = \mu_0 nI\,\pi r_s^2\]

Step 2 — numbers. \(B = (4\pi\times10^{-7})(1000)(3.00) = 3.77\) mT, and

\[\boxed{\;\Phi_B = (3.77\times10^{-3}\ \text{T})\,\pi(0.0500\ \text{m})^2 = 2.96\times10^{-5}\ \text{Wb} = 29.6\ \mu\text{Wb}\;}\]

\(r_\ell\) never entered. A loop of radius 15 cm or 1.5 m holds the same flux.

29.2 — Faraday’s Law

From the Experiment

Faraday’s measurements, and Henry’s, fix three things about the EMF induced in a coil. It is proportional to how fast the flux changes, not to the flux itself. It is proportional to the number of turns \(N\), since each turn adds its own EMF in series. And it opposes the change that drives it — the minus sign, which §29.3 takes up.

\[\boxed{\;\mathcal E = -N\,\frac{d\Phi_B}{dt}\;}\]

This is Faraday’s law of induction. It is found by experiment, as Coulomb’s law was; nothing earlier in the course produces it.

Three Ways to Change the Flux

\(\Phi_B = BA\cos\theta\) changes if any one of its three factors changes (Figure 29.2). The law does not care which.

  1. Change \(B\) — ramp the current in a nearby electromagnet (the wireless charger below).
  2. Change \(A\) — slide one side of a circuit (the rail, §29.4).
  3. Change \(\theta\) — turn the loop in a steady field (the generator, below).

The Field Form: Law (3)

The EMF around a circuit is the work per unit charge done going once around it (Chapter 26), which is the circulation of \(\vec E\). For one loop, Faraday’s law reads

\[\boxed{\;\oint\vec E\cdot d\vec\ell = -\frac{d\Phi_B}{dt}\;}\]

This is law (3) of §31.1. Compare Chapter 24, where \(\oint\vec E\cdot d\vec\ell = 0\) for the field of static charges. A changing magnetic flux makes an electric field whose circulation is not zero — a field that loops around and has no potential, so “the voltage between two points” depends on the path taken. That is why an induced EMF has no terminals: it is spread around the whole loop.

Check the result.

  • Steady flux. \(d\Phi_B/dt = 0\) gives \(\mathcal E = 0\), however large the field: the magnet sitting still in Faraday’s coil.
  • Units. \(\text{Wb/s} = \text{T}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}\). With \(\text{T} = \text{N}/(\text{A}\cdot\text{m})\) (Chapter 28), this is \(\text{N}\cdot\text{m}/(\text{A}\cdot\text{s}) = \text{J/C} = \text{V}\).
  • Turns. \(N\) identical turns in series give \(N\) times one turn’s EMF, the rule for batteries in series (Chapter 27).

Example: A Field That Ramps Up

A single circular loop of radius \(r\) and resistance \(R\) lies perpendicular to a uniform field that rises steadily from \(B_i\) to \(B_f\) in a time \(\Delta t\). Find the induced EMF and current for \(r = 8.00\) cm, \(R = 0.500\ \Omega\), \(B_i = 0.200\) T, \(B_f = 0.800\) T, \(\Delta t = 0.500\) s.

Why it matters: the pad’s changing field and the phone’s coil are what can be measured; the EMF and current delivered to the phone are what is wanted. This is a wireless charging pad: power across a gap, with no contacts.

Step 1 — symbols. Only \(B\) changes, so \(d\Phi_B/dt = \pi r^2\,dB/dt\), with \(dB/dt = (B_f - B_i)/\Delta t\):

\[|\mathcal E| = \pi r^2\,\frac{B_f - B_i}{\Delta t}, \qquad I = \frac{|\mathcal E|}{R}\]

Step 2 — numbers.

\[\boxed{\;|\mathcal E| = \pi(0.0800\ \text{m})^2\,\frac{0.600\ \text{T}}{0.500\ \text{s}} = 24.1\ \text{mV}, \qquad I = \frac{24.1\ \text{mV}}{0.500\ \Omega} = 48.2\ \text{mA}\;}\]

The direction comes from Lenz’s law (§29.3).

Example: The Generator

A coil of \(N\) turns and area \(A\) turns at angular speed \(\omega\) in a uniform field \(B\). Find the EMF as a function of time, and its peak, for \(N = 100\), \(A = 0.0200\ \text{m}^2\), \(B = 0.500\) T, \(\omega = 120\pi\) rad/s (60 Hz).

Why it matters: the turns, the field, the area and the turning rate are what a builder controls; the peak EMF is what comes out. The sinusoid of household power is not a design choice; it is what a turning coil makes.

Step 1 — the flux. The angle grows as \(\theta = \omega t\):

\[\Phi_B = BA\cos\omega t\]

Step 2 — differentiate. The derivative of \(\cos\omega t\) is \(-\omega\sin\omega t\):

\[\mathcal E = -N\frac{d\Phi_B}{dt} = NBA\omega\sin\omega t = \mathcal E_0\sin\omega t\]

Step 3 — numbers.

\[\boxed{\;\mathcal E_0 = NBA\omega = (100)(0.500\ \text{T})(0.0200\ \text{m}^2)(120\pi\ \text{s}^{-1}) = 377\ \text{V}\;}\]

Check the limits.

  • Face-on (\(\omega t = 0\)). The flux is largest but momentarily not changing, so \(\mathcal E = 0\). Most flux is not most EMF.
  • Edge-on (\(\omega t = \pi/2\)). The flux is zero but changing fastest, so \(\mathcal E = \mathcal E_0\).
  • Faster turning. \(\mathcal E_0 \propto \omega\): spin it twice as fast and the peak doubles, along with the frequency.

29.3 — Lenz’s Law

The Direction

Faraday’s law gives the size of the EMF. The minus sign gives its direction:

Lenz’s law: the induced current flows in the direction whose own magnetic field opposes the change in flux that produced it.

Why It Must Be So

Suppose the induced current reinforced the change instead. A small increase in flux would drive a current whose field increased the flux further, which would drive more current, and so on: a current and field growing without limit from a nudge, with nothing paying for the energy. Opposition is the only direction consistent with energy conservation. Whoever changes the flux has to push against the induced current, and that work is the electrical energy that appears.

A Recipe

  1. Find the direction of the external \(\vec B\) through the loop.
  2. Decide whether the flux is increasing or decreasing.
  3. The induced field opposes the change: against the external field if the flux is increasing, along it if decreasing.
  4. Use the right-hand rule (§28.4) to find the current that makes that induced field.

The bar magnet and the loop. Push a north pole toward a loop (Figure 29.3a). The magnet’s field through the loop points away from the pole and is increasing, so the induced field points back toward the magnet. Seen from the magnet, the induced current runs counterclockwise, and the loop’s near face is a north pole: the loop repels the incoming magnet. Pull the magnet away (Figure 29.3b) and everything reverses: the loop attracts it and resists the departure. Either way you push against the loop, in and out, and that work is what the induced current turns into heat in the wire.

Example: A Loop Around a Solenoid, Current Rising

A loop surrounds a solenoid whose field points to the right through the loop. The solenoid’s current is increasing. Find the direction of the induced current.

Why it matters: the solenoid’s field and whether its current is rising are known; the direction of the outer loop’s current is what is wanted. The supply driving the solenoid feels that current, since some of its work now goes into the outer loop. Every transformer (§29.5) works by this coupling.

Step 1 — the change. The flux to the right is increasing.

Step 2 — the induced field. It opposes the increase, so it points to the left inside the loop.

Step 3 — the current. A field to the left needs a current that runs clockwise as seen from the right (right-hand rule: thumb to the left, fingers curl clockwise for an observer looking from the right).

\[\boxed{\;\text{clockwise, seen from the right}\;}\]

29.4 — Motional EMF

Where the EMF Comes From: \(q\vec v\times\vec B\)

Faraday’s law covers a conductor that moves through a steady field, and here Chapter 28 says why.

Step 1 — the force on the rod’s charges. A rod of length \(L\) moves at \(\vec v\) perpendicular to \(\vec B\) (Figure 29.4). Every charge in it moves with it and feels \(q\vec v\times\vec B\) (§28.2), along the rod: with \(\vec v\) to the right and \(\vec B\) into the page, positive charge is pushed up.

Step 2 — charge piles up until the forces balance. The top end turns positive and the bottom negative. Their electric field pushes back, and the separation stops when

\[qE = qvB \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad E = vB\]

Step 3 — the potential difference. A uniform field \(E\) along a length \(L\) gives \(\Delta V = EL\) (Chapter 24):

\[\boxed{\;\mathcal E = BLv\;}\]

This is the motional EMF: no battery and no changing field, only a conductor moving through a steady one.

The Rail: Two Routes Agree

A rod slides at constant speed \(v\) along two rails a distance \(L\) apart, joined at one end through a resistor \(R\), in a uniform field into the page (Figure 29.5).

Step 1 — the flux. With the rod a distance \(x\) from the resistor, the circuit encloses \(A = Lx\):

\[\Phi_B = BLx\]

Step 2 — Faraday’s law. Only \(x\) changes, at \(dx/dt = v\):

\[|\mathcal E| = \frac{d\Phi_B}{dt} = BLv\]

the same as the force route. One law, two pictures.

Step 3 — the current and its direction. \(I = BLv/R\). The flux into the page is increasing, so the induced field points out of the page, and the current runs counterclockwise — up the rod, as Step 1 of the force route found.

Step 4 — the braking force. The rod now carries \(I\) across \(\vec B\), so it feels \(F = ILB\) (§28.3). Its direction, \(I\vec L\times\vec B\) with the current up and the field into the page, is to the left: against the motion, as Lenz’s law requires.

\[F = ILB = \frac{B^2L^2v}{R}\]

Step 5 — who pays. To keep \(v\) constant, an agent must push with \(F\), supplying power \(Fv\). The resistor turns electrical energy into heat at \(I^2R\):

\[Fv = \frac{B^2L^2v^2}{R}, \qquad I^2R = \left(\frac{BLv}{R}\right)^2 R = \frac{B^2L^2v^2}{R}\]

\[\boxed{\;\mathcal E = BLv, \qquad I = \frac{BLv}{R}, \qquad F = \frac{B^2L^2v}{R}, \qquad Fv = I^2R\;}\]

Every joule the agent supplies ends up as heat in the resistor. The speed is constant, so none of it goes into kinetic energy.

Check the limits.

  • \(v \to 0\). No EMF, no current, no force: a resting rod is just a wire.
  • \(R \to \infty\) (the circuit is broken). The EMF \(BLv\) is still there across the rod’s ends, but no current flows and the rod slides freely.
  • Reverse \(\vec B\). The current reverses and the field reverses, so \(F \propto B^2\) is unchanged: the force still opposes the motion.
  • Faster. \(F \propto v\) and the power \(\propto v^2\): twice the speed, twice the force, four times the power.

Example: Rod on Rails

Find the EMF, the current, the force needed to keep the rod moving, and the power balance, for \(v = 5.00\) m/s, \(L = 0.400\) m, \(B = 0.800\) T, \(R = 2.00\ \Omega\).

Why it matters: the speed, the field and the rod’s length are measurable; the braking force and the power recovered are what is wanted. This is regenerative braking stripped to its parts. Because \(F \propto v\), the braking is strong at speed and fades as the car slows, which is why an electric car still carries friction brakes for the last few meters.

Step 1 — symbols. From the boxed results above: \(\mathcal E = BLv\), \(I = \mathcal E/R\), \(F = ILB\), and \(Fv\) against \(I^2R\).

Step 2 — numbers.

\[\boxed{\;\begin{aligned} \mathcal E &= (0.800\ \text{T})(0.400\ \text{m})(5.00\ \text{m/s}) = 1.60\ \text{V}, \qquad I = \frac{1.60\ \text{V}}{2.00\ \Omega} = 0.800\ \text{A}\\ F &= (0.800\ \text{A})(0.400\ \text{m})(0.800\ \text{T}) = 0.256\ \text{N}\\ Fv &= (0.256\ \text{N})(5.00\ \text{m/s}) = 1.28\ \text{W} = (0.800\ \text{A})^2(2.00\ \Omega) = I^2R \end{aligned}\;}\]

A Loop Crossing a Field Region

A closed loop that moves through a region of field, rather than sliding on rails, shows when induction happens and when it does not. A square loop of side \(\ell\) and resistance \(R\) moves at constant \(v\) through a region of uniform field out of the page, of width \(D > \ell\) (Figure 29.6).

Why it matters: the loop’s speed and the width of the field region are set; when the loop is braked, and how hard, is what is wanted. A roller coaster’s magnetic brakes are copper fins on the cars passing between rows of magnets, so the braking can be placed exactly, with nothing touching.

Step 1 — entering. With the leading edge a distance \(x < \ell\) into the region, the field fills an area \(\ell x\) of the loop: \(\Phi_B = B\ell x\), rising at \(B\ell v\).

\[|\mathcal E| = B\ell v, \qquad I = \frac{B\ell v}{R}\]

The flux out of the page is increasing, so the induced field points into the page: the current runs clockwise.

Step 2 — fully inside. The whole loop is in the field: \(\Phi_B = B\ell^2\), which is not changing. No EMF, no current. In the force picture, both vertical sides now move through the field and each has an EMF \(B\ell v\), but the two push charge the same way in space — so around the loop they oppose, and cancel.

Step 3 — leaving. The flux falls at \(B\ell v\), so the EMF has the same size and the current runs the other way, counterclockwise.

\[\boxed{\;|\mathcal E| = NB\ell v \ \ \text{entering or leaving}, \qquad \mathcal E = 0 \ \ \text{fully inside or fully outside}\;}\]

A coil of \(N\) turns has \(N\) such loops in series, hence the \(N\). The side in the field then carries \(NI\) across it, and the force on that side is \(NI\ell B\).

Check the result.

  • The force always opposes the motion. Entering, the current is clockwise and the side in the field is the leading one; leaving, the current reverses but the side in the field is now the trailing one. Both flips together leave the force pointing backward — Lenz’s law each time.
  • Inside, the loop coasts. No current means no magnetic force. Uniform field alone does not slow the loop; only changing flux does.
  • Reverse the field. Every current direction reverses; the sizes do not.

Eddy Currents

A solid sheet of metal moving through a field is a crowd of loops at once. The changing flux drives swirling eddy currents in the metal (Figure 29.7), each obeying Lenz’s law. They push back on the motion and heat the metal as \(I^2R\).

  • Magnetic braking: a strong magnet dropped down a copper pipe falls slowly, with no contact.
  • Induction cooktops: a rapidly alternating field drives eddy currents in the pan, which heats; the glass top does not.
  • Metal detectors: eddy currents in a buried object change the field of the detector’s coil.

Example: A Magnet Falling Through a Copper Pipe

A magnet of mass \(m\) falls down a vertical copper pipe at a steady terminal speed \(v_t\). Find the power dissipated in the pipe for \(m = 5.00\) g, \(v_t = 0.100\) m/s.

Why it matters: the mass and the terminal speed are easy to measure with a ruler and a stopwatch; the heating power in the pipe is not. The rail’s energy balance, \(Fv = I^2R\), turns one into the other.

Step 1 — symbols. At terminal speed the magnetic drag balances gravity, \(F = mg\), and the drag does work on the magnet at the rate \(Fv_t\). The magnet’s kinetic energy is not changing, so all of it goes into the pipe:

\[P = mg\,v_t\]

Step 2 — numbers.

\[\boxed{\;P = (0.00500\ \text{kg})(9.80\ \text{m/s}^2)(0.100\ \text{m/s}) = 4.90\ \text{mW}\;}\]

29.5 — Inductance

Faraday’s Law Applied to a Coil’s Own Flux

A coil carrying current makes a field, and that field passes through the coil’s own turns. Change the current and the coil’s own flux changes, so Faraday’s law induces an EMF in the coil itself.

Step 1 — the flux linkage is proportional to the current. Every field a current makes is proportional to it (Chapter 28; for a solenoid, \(B = \mu_0 nI\)), so \(N\Phi_B \propto I\). The constant of proportionality depends only on the coil’s shape. Call it the inductance:

\[L = \frac{N\Phi_B}{I} \qquad (1\ \text{henry} = 1\ \text{H} = 1\ \text{Wb/A} = 1\ \text{V}\cdot\text{s/A})\]

Step 2 — Faraday’s law. With \(N\Phi_B = LI\):

\[\boxed{\;L = \frac{N\Phi_B}{I}, \qquad \mathcal E_L = -\frac{d(N\Phi_B)}{dt} = -L\,\frac{dI}{dt}\;}\]

By Lenz’s law the self-induced EMF opposes the change in current: it pushes back while the current rises, and pushes forward while it falls.

An inductor is a flywheel for current. A flywheel resists any change in how fast it spins; once spinning it keeps going, and starting or stopping it takes effort. An inductor does the same to the current through it. A steady current costs the inductor nothing (\(dI/dt = 0\), no EMF); it is the change that meets resistance.

Flywheel Inductor
rotational inertia inductance \(L\)
angular speed \(\omega\) current \(I\)
torque needed \(\propto d\omega/dt\) EMF needed \(= L\,dI/dt\)
keeps spinning once started keeps the current flowing once started

The Inductance of a Solenoid

A solenoid of length \(\ell\), cross-section \(A\) and \(n\) turns per meter (\(N = n\ell\) turns in all):

Step 1 — the field and the flux per turn. \(B = \mu_0 nI\) (§28.6), so each turn holds \(\Phi_B = \mu_0 nIA\).

Step 2 — the flux linkage. \(N\Phi_B = (n\ell)(\mu_0 nIA) = \mu_0 n^2\ell A\,I\).

Step 3 — divide by \(I\).

\[\boxed{\;L = \mu_0 n^2\ell A\;}\]

Check the result.

  • No current in the answer. \(L\) depends on the coil’s shape alone, as \(C\) depends on the capacitor’s shape alone (\(C = \varepsilon_0 A/d\), Chapter 25).
  • \(n^2\). Doubling the turns per meter doubles the field and doubles the number of turns it threads: four times the inductance.
  • Units. \(\mu_0 n^2\ell A\): \(\frac{\text{T}\cdot\text{m}}{\text{A}}\cdot\frac{1}{\text{m}^2}\cdot\text{m}\cdot\text{m}^2 = \frac{\text{T}\cdot\text{m}^2}{\text{A}} = \text{Wb/A} = \text{H}\).

Example: A Lab Inductor

A solenoid has \(N\) turns on a length \(\ell\) with radius \(r\). Find its inductance, and the EMF across it when the current changes at a rate \(dI/dt\), for \(N = 500\), \(\ell = 0.250\) m, \(r = 2.00\) cm, \(dI/dt = 200\) A/s.

Why it matters: a ruler and a turn count give the inductance before the coil is ever powered, the same design move as \(C = \varepsilon_0 A/d\). The EMF it makes when the current changes is what the rest of the circuit feels.

Step 1 — symbols. \(n = N/\ell\) and \(A = \pi r^2\):

\[L = \mu_0\left(\frac{N}{\ell}\right)^2\ell\,\pi r^2 = \frac{\mu_0N^2\pi r^2}{\ell}, \qquad |\mathcal E_L| = L\,\frac{dI}{dt}\]

Step 2 — numbers.

\[\boxed{\;L = \frac{(4\pi\times10^{-7})(500)^2\,\pi(0.0200\ \text{m})^2}{0.250\ \text{m}} = 1.58\ \text{mH}, \qquad |\mathcal E_L| = (1.58\times10^{-3}\ \text{H})(200\ \text{A/s}) = 0.316\ \text{V}\;}\]

Millihenrys are typical of electronics; a slow change in current barely registers.

Example: Switching Off an Inductive Load

A relay coil with \(L = 50.0\) mH and winding resistance \(R = 2.00\ \Omega\) runs from a \(6.00\) V supply. A switch opens and stops the current in \(\Delta t = 0.100\) ms. Estimate the EMF across the coil.

Why it matters: the inductance, the current and the switching time are known; the voltage across the opening contacts is what is wanted. That voltage is why every relay and motor driver carries a flyback diode across the coil, giving the current a closed path to die away gradually (§29.6 finds how fast). A car’s ignition coil does the opposite on purpose: it interrupts its current to make the spark.

Step 1 — the steady current. \(I = \mathcal E/R\), since a steady current meets no opposition from \(L\).

Step 2 — the kick. The current falls from \(I\) to zero in \(\Delta t\), so on average

\[|\mathcal E_L| = L\,\frac{\Delta I}{\Delta t} = \frac{L\,(\mathcal E/R)}{\Delta t}\]

Step 3 — numbers.

\[\boxed{\;I = \frac{6.00\ \text{V}}{2.00\ \Omega} = 3.00\ \text{A}, \qquad |\mathcal E_L| = (0.0500\ \text{H})\,\frac{3.00\ \text{A}}{1.00\times10^{-4}\ \text{s}} = 1500\ \text{V}\;}\]

Two hundred fifty times the supply voltage. The flywheel will not stop on a dime: the coil makes whatever EMF it takes to keep the current going, and here that EMF jumps the gap of the opening switch as a spark.

Mutual Inductance and the Transformer

When two coils share flux, a changing current in one induces an EMF in the other: \(\mathcal E_2 = -M\,dI_1/dt\), where the mutual inductance \(M\) depends on the coils’ shapes and placement.

A transformer winds two coils on one iron core, which carries the same flux \(\Phi_B\) through every turn of both. Faraday’s law on each coil:

\[\mathcal E_1 = -N_1\frac{d\Phi_B}{dt}, \qquad \mathcal E_2 = -N_2\frac{d\Phi_B}{dt} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \frac{\mathcal E_2}{\mathcal E_1} = \frac{N_2}{N_1}\]

The voltage steps by the turns ratio — but only for a changing current, which is why the grid runs on alternating current. Stepping up to high voltage for transmission lowers the current, and the \(I^2R\) lost in the lines falls with its square.

The inductor is the capacitor’s partner.

Capacitor (Ch 25) Inductor (Ch 29)
Defined by \(C = Q/\Delta V\) \(L = N\Phi_B/I\)
Ideal shape \(C = \varepsilon_0A/d\) \(L = \mu_0n^2\ell A\)
Stores energy in the electric field the magnetic field (§29.6)
Resists a change in its voltage its current
In a steady DC circuit an open switch a plain wire

29.6 — RL Circuits

Current Growth

A battery \(\mathcal E\), a resistor \(R\) and an inductor \(L\) are in series. At \(t = 0\) the switch closes (Figure 29.8).

Step 1 — the loop rule at time \(t\). Going around with the current, the resistor drops \(IR\) and the inductor, opposing the rising current, drops \(L\,dI/dt\):

\[\mathcal E - IR - L\,\frac{dI}{dt} = 0\]

Step 2 — the bridging step: it is Chapter 27’s equation. Rearranged, the RC charging equation of §27.4 and this one have the same shape:

\[\text{RC:}\quad \frac{dq}{dt} = \frac{C\mathcal E - q}{RC}, \qquad\qquad \text{RL:}\quad \frac{dI}{dt} = \frac{\mathcal E/R - I}{L/R}\]

Each says: the quantity climbs toward a final value at a rate proportional to how far it still has to go. The final value is \(C\mathcal E\) for the charge and \(\mathcal E/R\) for the current; the time scale is \(RC\) in one and \(L/R\) in the other.

Step 3 — the same equation has the same solution. Section 27.4 solved the first (Steps 3–5 there). Replace \(q \to I\), \(C\mathcal E \to \mathcal E/R\) and \(RC \to L/R\):

\[\boxed{\;I(t) = \frac{\mathcal E}{R}\left(1 - e^{-t/\tau}\right), \qquad \tau = \frac{L}{R}\;}\]

Step 4 — the inductor’s EMF. Differentiate: \(L\,dI/dt = \mathcal E\,e^{-t/\tau}\). At the start the whole battery EMF sits across the inductor; it fades as the current builds.

Check the limits.

  • At \(t = 0\): \(I = 0\) and the whole EMF is across \(L\). An inductor meeting a sudden voltage acts like an open switch — the reverse of an uncharged capacitor, which acts like a wire.
  • As \(t \to \infty\): \(I \to \mathcal E/R\) and \(L\,dI/dt \to 0\). A steady-state inductor is a plain wire.
  • Larger \(L\) is slower; more flywheel. Larger \(R\) is faster — the reverse of RC. A larger \(R\) sets a smaller final current \(\mathcal E/R\), so there is less current to build.
  • Units. \(\text{H}/\Omega = (\text{V}\cdot\text{s/A})/(\text{V/A}) = \text{s}\).

Current Decay

With a steady current \(I_0\) flowing, the battery is switched out and the coil is left closed through \(R\). The loop rule is \(L\,dI/dt + IR = 0\), the RL partner of RC discharge (§27.4), with the same answer:

\[\boxed{\;I(t) = I_0\,e^{-t/\tau}, \qquad \tau = \frac{L}{R}\;}\]

RC (Ch 27) RL (Ch 29)
What climbs charge \(q\) current \(I\)
Final value \(C\mathcal E\) \(\mathcal E/R\)
Time constant \(RC\) \(L/R\)
Element at \(t = 0\) a wire an open switch
Element at \(t \to \infty\) an open switch a wire
Larger \(R\) slower faster

Energy Stored in an Inductor

Step 1 — the power to push current against the inductor. While the current rises, the inductor’s EMF \(L\,dI/dt\) opposes it, and the circuit must deliver power \(P = I \cdot L\,dI/dt\) to keep it rising.

Step 2 — the work for each small step in current. In time \(dt\) the current rises by \(dI\), and the work done is

\[dW = P\,dt = LI\,dI\]

Step 3 — add up the steps: a triangle. \(LI\) plotted against \(I\) is a straight line through the origin (Figure 29.10), so the total work from zero to \(I\) is the area of a triangle, half the enclosing rectangle — exactly the argument of Chapter 25, where \(\Delta V = q/C\) against \(q\) gave \(\tfrac12C(\Delta V)^2\).

\[\boxed{\;U_B = \tfrac12 LI^2\;}\]

The energy is stored, not lost: when the current falls, the inductor gives it back. It is the flywheel’s \(\tfrac12(\text{inertia})\,\omega^2\), the spring’s \(\tfrac12kx^2\), and the capacitor’s \(\tfrac12C(\Delta V)^2\).

Where the Energy Lives: \(u_B\)

Section 31.5 used the magnetic energy density \(u_B = B^2/2\mu_0\) as stated. The solenoid derives it, as the parallel-plate capacitor derived \(u_E = \tfrac12\varepsilon_0E^2\) in Chapter 25.

Step 1 — write \(U_B\) in terms of the field. For a solenoid, \(L = \mu_0 n^2\ell A\) and \(B = \mu_0 nI\), so \(I = B/\mu_0 n\):

\[U_B = \tfrac12(\mu_0 n^2\ell A)\left(\frac{B}{\mu_0 n}\right)^2 = \frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}\,(\ell A)\]

Step 2 — divide by the volume. The field is uniform inside the solenoid and negligible outside, so the energy fills the volume \(\ell A\) evenly:

\[\boxed{\;u_B = \frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}\;}\]

Back in §31.5, this with \(u_E = \tfrac12\varepsilon_0E^2\) and \(E = cB\) showed that a light wave carries exactly half its energy in each field. That step now rests on a derivation.

Check the result.

  • Units. \(\frac{\text{T}^2}{\text{T}\cdot\text{m/A}} = \frac{\text{T}\cdot\text{A}}{\text{m}} = \frac{\text{N}}{\text{A}\cdot\text{m}}\cdot\frac{\text{A}}{\text{m}} = \frac{\text{N}}{\text{m}^2} = \frac{\text{J}}{\text{m}^3}\).
  • Two routes, one number. The lab inductor of §29.5 at 3.00 A has \(B = \mu_0(2000)(3.00) = 7.54\) mT, \(u_B = 22.6\ \text{J/m}^3\), and a volume \(\ell A = 3.14\times10^{-4}\ \text{m}^3\), so \(U_B = 7.11\) mJ — the same as \(\tfrac12LI^2 = \tfrac12(1.58\ \text{mH})(3.00\ \text{A})^2\).

Example: Energy in an RL Circuit

\(\mathcal E = 24.0\) V, \(R = 8.00\ \Omega\), \(L = 4.00\) H; the switch closes at \(t = 0\). Find the time constant, the final current, the current at \(t = \tau\), the energy stored at steady state, and the power in \(R\) at \(t = \tau\).

Why it matters: \(L\) and \(R\) are measurable; the response time is what is designed for. Because a larger \(R\) makes \(\tau\) shorter, a solenoid valve that must snap open fast is often driven at a higher voltage through a series resistor: the same final current, reached sooner.

Step 1 — symbols.

\[\tau = \frac{L}{R}, \quad I_\text{max} = \frac{\mathcal E}{R}, \quad I(\tau) = I_\text{max}(1 - e^{-1}), \quad U_B = \tfrac12LI_\text{max}^2, \quad P_R = I(\tau)^2R\]

Step 2 — numbers.

\[\boxed{\;\begin{aligned} \tau &= \frac{4.00\ \text{H}}{8.00\ \Omega} = 0.500\ \text{s}, \qquad I_\text{max} = \frac{24.0\ \text{V}}{8.00\ \Omega} = 3.00\ \text{A}, \qquad I(\tau) = (3.00\ \text{A})(0.632) = 1.90\ \text{A}\\ U_B &= \tfrac12(4.00\ \text{H})(3.00\ \text{A})^2 = 18.0\ \text{J}, \qquad P_R = (1.90\ \text{A})^2(8.00\ \Omega) = 28.8\ \text{W} \end{aligned}\;}\]

At steady state the resistor takes the battery’s full \(72.0\) W, and the inductor holds its 18.0 J without taking any more.

Example: The Relay Coil, Revisited

Return to the relay coil of §29.5 (\(L = 50.0\) mH, \(R = 2.00\ \Omega\), \(I = 3.00\) A). With a flyback diode, the current dies away through the coil’s own resistance. Find the time constant and the energy the coil must get rid of.

Why it matters: \(L\) and \(I\) fix how much energy the coil holds; the diode or the switch decides how fast it comes out, and the rate is what does the damage.

Step 1 — symbols. \(\tau = L/R\) and \(U_B = \tfrac12LI^2\).

Step 2 — numbers.

\[\boxed{\;\tau = \frac{0.0500\ \text{H}}{2.00\ \Omega} = 25.0\ \text{ms}, \qquad U_B = \tfrac12(0.0500\ \text{H})(3.00\ \text{A})^2 = 0.225\ \text{J}\;}\]

The energy is the same either way; the time is not. Released over about \(25\) ms through the diode, \(0.225\) J is roughly 9 W for a moment, which a small diode handles. Forced out in the switch’s \(0.100\) ms, it is about 2 kW, delivered as the spark.

29.7 — The Speed of Light from Laws (3) and (4)

Section 31.3 stated that laws (3) and (4), applied to a front of field moving into empty space, fix its speed at \(c = 1/\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}\) and fix \(E = cB\). With Faraday’s law in hand, the derivation takes one loop for each law.

Why it matters: the two constants are measured on a lab bench: \(\varepsilon_0\) from a capacitor (Chapter 25) and \(\mu_0\) from the force between two wires (§28.5). The speed of light is what comes out. No optics go in, which is how Maxwell, in 1862, concluded that light is an electromagnetic wave.

The setup. A flat front moves in the \(+x\) direction at an unknown speed \(v\). Behind it, there is a uniform \(\vec E\) along \(y\) and a uniform \(\vec B\) along \(z\); ahead of it, no field yet. There are no charges and no currents anywhere (Figure 29.11).

Step 1 — law (3), the flux. Take a rectangular loop of height \(h\) in the \(x\)–\(y\) plane, straddling the front (Figure 29.11a). In time \(dt\) the front advances \(v\,dt\), adding an area \(hv\,dt\) of field \(B\) inside the loop:

\[\frac{d\Phi_B}{dt} = Bhv\]

Step 2 — law (3), the circulation. Along the loop’s top and bottom, \(\vec E\) is perpendicular to the path and contributes nothing. The side ahead of the front has no field. Only the side behind it, of length \(h\), counts:

\[\oint\vec E\cdot d\vec\ell = Eh\]

Step 3 — law (3) gives the first relation. Setting the two equal (sizes only):

\[Eh = Bhv \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad E = vB\]

Step 4 — law (4) gives the second. Repeat with a loop of height \(h\) in the \(x\)–\(z\) plane (Figure 29.11b). There is no current, so only Maxwell’s term is left. The electric flux grows at \(Ehv\); the circulation of \(\vec B\) is \(Bh\):

\[Bh = \mu_0\varepsilon_0\,Ehv \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad B = \mu_0\varepsilon_0\,vE\]

Step 5 — combine. Substitute the second into the first:

\[E = v\,(\mu_0\varepsilon_0\,vE) \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad v^2 = \frac{1}{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}\]

\[\boxed{\;v = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{(4\pi\times10^{-7})(8.854\times10^{-12})}} = 2.998\times10^8\ \text{m/s} = c, \qquad E = cB\;}\]

*Steps 3 and 4 used sizes only. Keeping the signs of laws (3) and (4) — each loop’s direction tied to its normal by the right-hand rule — gives the third result of §31.3, travel along \(\vec E\times\vec B\); that bookkeeping is not repeated here.

Check the result.

  • One speed only. \(E = vB\) and \(B = \mu_0\varepsilon_0vE\) can hold together with \(E \neq 0\) only if \(v^2 = 1/\mu_0\varepsilon_0\). At any other speed the two laws contradict each other, and there is no front.
  • No charges, no currents. Nothing in Steps 1–5 refers to a source. Once started, the pair of fields carries itself.
  • No wave shape. The front could be the leading edge of any pattern; the sinusoid of §31.4 is one choice, and every shape moves at the same \(c\).
  • \(E = cB\) is the \(E_0 = cB_0\) of §31.4.

29.8 — Maxwell’s Four Laws, Assembled

With Faraday’s law, every piece of classical electromagnetism has a chapter behind it:

Law Integral form Where it comes from
(1) Gauss \(\oint\vec E\cdot d\vec A = Q_\text{enc}/\varepsilon_0\) Ch 23
(2) Gauss, magnetic \(\oint\vec B\cdot d\vec A = 0\) Ch 28 (§28.7)
(3) Faraday \(\oint\vec E\cdot d\vec\ell = -\,d\Phi_B/dt\) Ch 29 (§29.2), stated in §31.1
(4) Ampère–Maxwell \(\oint\vec B\cdot d\vec\ell = \mu_0I_\text{enc} + \mu_0\varepsilon_0\,d\Phi_E/dt\) Ch 28 (§28.6) + Ch 31 (§31.2)

Laws (1) and (2) say where fields come from: electric field lines start on charge, and magnetic field lines never start at all. Laws (3) and (4) say how the two fields make each other when something changes — and §29.7 showed that those two alone, with no charge or current anywhere, carry a front of field across empty space at \(c\). The light of Chapters 30 and 31 is in these four lines.

29.9 — Summary

Key Concepts

  1. Magnetic flux \(\Phi_B = BA\cos\theta\) measures the field threading a loop; it counts only where the field is. \(N\Phi_B\) is the flux linkage.
  2. Faraday’s law: a changing flux induces \(\mathcal E = -N\,d\Phi_B/dt\). Only change matters — a change in \(B\), in area, or in angle. In field form it is law (3): the induced \(\vec E\) circulates and has no potential.
  3. Lenz’s law: the induced current opposes the change that made it. The minus sign is energy conservation; whoever changes the flux does the work.
  4. Motional EMF \(\mathcal E = BLv\) comes from \(q\vec v\times\vec B\) on the moving conductor’s charges, and agrees with Faraday’s law. On the rail, \(F = B^2L^2v/R\) opposes the motion and \(Fv = I^2R\).
  5. A loop crossing a field region carries current only while entering or leaving, in opposite directions; fully inside, the flux is steady and there is none.
  6. Inductance \(L = N\Phi_B/I\) is Faraday’s law applied to a coil’s own flux: \(\mathcal E_L = -L\,dI/dt\). For a solenoid \(L = \mu_0n^2\ell A\). An inductor is a flywheel for current.
  7. RL circuits obey RC’s equation with \(q \to I\) and \(RC \to L/R\): the current climbs as \((\mathcal E/R)(1 - e^{-t/\tau})\) and decays as \(I_0e^{-t/\tau}\), with \(\tau = L/R\).
  8. Energy: \(U_B = \tfrac12LI^2\), from the triangle under \(LI\); in the field, \(u_B = B^2/2\mu_0\).
  9. The speed of light follows from laws (3) and (4) applied to a moving front: \(c = 1/\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}\) and \(E = cB\).

Looking Back

The course opened in Chapter 22 with Coulomb’s law: two charges at rest, one force between them. It closes with four field laws that hold everything since — the fields of charges (Chapters 22–25), the circuits that move charge (Chapters 26–27), the magnetic fields of moving charge (Chapter 28), and the induction of this chapter. Run two of those laws against each other in empty space and they produce light (§29.7), which is where Chapters 30 and 31 began. Every generator, transformer, motor, radio and fiber-optic link is an application of the four lines in §29.8.
